chunks: What PCB rework is. The question: What is PCB rework?
PCB rework means going back to a board that is already built and changing it. You take a part off, put a new one on, or fix a bad connection.
It exists because boards sometimes come out wrong, and fixing one is often cheaper than scrapping it.
The catch is that rework melts the solder again, so the board gets another dose of heat it has to survive.
Imagine fixing one brick in a wall whose mortar has already set.
You have to soften the mortar around that brick without loosening its neighbors, and each repair leaves the wall a little weaker. A cheap wall you would just rebuild.
A board works the same way, except that solder really can be melted again, which is what makes the fix possible at all.
Rework is a loop with an economic gate at the start (is it worth it?) and an inspection gate at the end.
A failed inspection sends you back around, adding another thermal cycle to the board.
Solder: a metal that melts at a fairly low temperature and joins a part to the board. Pad: the small copper patch on the board that a part is soldered to.
Flux: a paste that cleans the metal so melted solder sticks to it. Preheat: warming the whole board gently first, so it is not shocked by local heat.
Rework, repair, modification: rework restores the original design, repair fixes damage, and modification deliberately changes the design.
A built board has a resistor of the wrong value. You put flux on it, preheat the board, and heat the part until its solder melts.
Common lead-free solder melts at about 217 degrees Celsius. You lift the part off, clean the pads, solder on the right resistor, and check it.
That second dose of heat is the cost of the fix. That is the whole idea.
"Rework is removing, replacing or modifying parts or connections on a board that's already been assembled.
Usually that's desoldering a bad component and soldering in a new one, or adding jumper wires for a design change.
It needs a controlled thermal profile, flux, preheat and ESD care, because every rework cycle stresses the pads and laminate.
It's a last resort that gets weighed against scrapping the board, and good layout makes it easier."
